claims.text: Signature dishes include Miwa-somen tom yum kung, which uses wheat somen noodles, indicating wheat is handled in the kitchen.
Kakigori use dairy (yogurt cream, mimolette cheese) and Thai dishes typically use fish sauce, so vegan-safe preparation is not documented.
A vegetable yam (Thai salad) is made with produce from neighboring farms, and many non-spicy dishes are available, so vegetable-forward and mild options exist.

name: ラサ ボジュン 奈良店 (Rasa Bojun Nara)

claims.text: Staff can adjust spice level, and extra hot sauce is offered separately, so heat can be customized on request.
A vegetarian set is available, and the menu is built around multiple coconut-milk vegetable and lentil curries that suit plant-forward eating.
Curries are rice-based with saffron rice, which is naturally a non-wheat staple.

name: リストランテ リンコントロ (Ristorante Lincontro)

claims.text: The kitchen makes its own pasta and bread on-site, so flour is in heavy use and cross-contamination is likely; no gluten-free handling is documented.

Menus center on wild game and house-cured pork products, and the chef processes whole animals in-house, so shared surfaces and equipment make strict vegan separation unlikely without prior arrangement.
Small 15-seat, reservation-only course format means the chef can be told of dietary needs in advance and can tailor a meal around seasonal Yamato vegetables.

name: 路地裏のおにぎり屋さん 一穂二穂 (Rojiura no Onigiri-yasan Ippo Niho)

claims.text: Several fillings are soy-sauce based (for example egg-yolk soy sauce), and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.
The owner simmers broths from multiple kinds of fish and many fillings are meat or egg, so animal ingredients are prepared in the same small kitchen.

Owner-made food with carefully selected, simple core ingredients (a chosen rice, Ariake nori, Goto salt) and a stated avoidance of chemical seasonings, so the owner can usually explain exactly what is in each onigiri.

name: ロクメイコーヒー 奈良店 (Rokumei Coffee Co. Nara)

claims.text: Wheat croissants and pastries are baked and handled on-site, so gluten is present in the kitchen; no gluten-free protocol is documented.
Butter croissants and dairy/egg pastries are central to the menu; no separate vegan preparation is documented, so plant-based items risk dairy contact.
Plain black hand-drip and specialty coffee is naturally gluten-free and vegan, and the baristas brew each cup to order.
Tabelog lists vegetarian-friendly and 'particular about vegetables' tags for the shop.
Wheat noodles (udon and nyūmen/somen) are central to the menu and are cooked in shared kitchen space; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
Broths are dashi/soy-based; standard Japanese soy sauce containing wheat should be assumed. No wheat-free soy sauce is documented.
Noodle broths use fish dashi and the menu mixes dairy (milk syrup) and animal-free items; vegans should ask which kakigori syrups and toppings are dairy- and animal-free.

Shaved ice is made with pure ice and house-made syrups using Nara ingredients, with some plant-leaning options like kinako, honey/mizore syrups, red bean paste, and house-made warabi mochi that a careful diner can ask about.
An English menu is available and vegetarian options are noted by an English tourism listing.
The signature chagayu is a rice-and-tea porridge accompanied by Yamato vegetables, pickles, and plums, so the core dish is plant- and rice-based.

The entire menu is prepared to halal standards, which means strict attention to what goes into each dish, and the owner runs the kitchen personally — making it practical to ask about ingredients directly.
Documented vegetable-forward and chickpea-based options exist, including falafel and shakshuka, alongside an emphasis on fresh produce.
Naturally gluten-free choices such as falafel, shakshuka and rice-based kebsa are on the menu, though cross-contamination is not documented.
